source.title: MoE Sparsity Begets Monosemanticity: Insights into Understanding and Fine-Tuning
source.authors: Ming-Xue Tian; Qi Zhang; Xiao-Han Wang; Jia-Jun Chai; Guo-Jun Yin; Wei Lin; Cai-Lian Chen; Qi-Min Xu; Si-Yu Wang; Yi-Sen Wang

record.tranche_reason: The study uses a different method to evaluate monosemanticity: natural-language explanations of MoE experts are used to predict expert activations, rather than counting neuron poles with one main job.
record.gate_note: The study measures MoE expert-level monosemanticity, not neuron-pole job shares. It does not report the Qwen3-32B audit percentages or test neuron explanations on held-out activations. Fine-tuning benchmark results are not rows because they measure adaptation performance, not monosemanticity.
record.test_reason: Every monosemanticity measurement is of whole MoE experts, not neurons or neuron poles. The study scores experts by asking GPT-4o to predict activations from explanations, then uses those scores to choose experts for fine-tuning. No version is tested: V1 and V2 name shares of neuron poles with one job, and V7 names automated scores of neuron explanations. Expert-level scores are a related but different construct. The only neuron result (Appendix A.10) is a few qualitative explanations, with no share or score.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that MoE sparsity promotes expert-level monosemanticity, middle layers specialize most, and experts are either domain-specific or general. Two additions: they also conclude that EDMRS expert-frozen fine-tuning matches or beats full fine-tuning in-domain while substantially improving out-of-domain retention, beating AF, LoRA and routerPEFT. Their claim that dense LLMs are less monosemantic is inferred from the k trend; no dense model was measured.
record.recipe_differences: Like automated neuron-interpretability work, the study generates natural-language explanations and evaluates them by predicting activations. It applies this pipeline to MoE experts, adds general and domain-specific scores, and reports no neuron-pole job-share audit.
record.method_sensitivity: LDS changes with the number of activated experts and network depth; EDMS differs from general EMS. Appendix A.12 reports LDS varying with explanation word limit.

fits_no_version.finding: In Qwen3-30B-A3B, raising k (lower routing sparsity) consistently lowers expert-level explain-and-predict accuracy (LDS) in four layers (figure only).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In MoE LLMs, higher routing sparsity yields more predictable (monosemantic) expert explanations.

fits_no_version.finding: In Qwen3-235B-A22B, expert LDS rises in early layers, plateaus in middle layers and drops near the output (figure only).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Expert monosemanticity in MoE LLMs peaks in middle layers.

fits_no_version.finding: Domain-constrained expert scores (EDMS) are generally lower than general scores (EMS). Some experts are domain-specialized, others are shared across domains.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: MoE experts split into domain-specialized and shared experts.

fits_no_version.finding: Expert 114 gets a domain-level explanation (medical textbook content), while its neurons get low-level token explanations (function words, numbers, angle-bracket content).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Expert explanations describe broader semantics than explanations of their constituent neurons.

fits_no_version.finding: In a middle layer, mean expert explain-and-predict accuracy (LDS) is about 0.69–0.71 across explanation word limits of 20–100 (Table 9). Rankings agree with a cheaper evaluator (Spearman 0.815 and 0.774) and with human annotators (0.701).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Automated explanation scoring of MoE experts gives moderate binary-prediction accuracy that is robust to the choice of evaluator.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026)
record.problems: The study's core measurements concern MoE experts rather than neuron poles, and it reports no neuron-pole job proportions. Numerical LDS values in the relevant plots are not stated in the text. The paper reports evaluator correlations, but those do not establish the claimed cross-model proportions.
record.rows_left_out: Fine-tuning comparisons and benchmark scores in Sections 5 and Appendices A.5–A.8 were left out because they measure adaptation performance rather than monosemanticity. Evaluator-replacement and human-annotator correlations in Section 5.1 and Appendix A.9 concern metric agreement, not the claimed neuron-pole shares.

untested.parts: All: no neuron-pole audit of Qwen3-32B.
All: no shares of neuron poles with one job in any model, dense or MoE. Only expert-level scores are reported.
All: no vision models and no cat/car neuron.
All: no test of tools or architecture versus capacity for neuron interpretability.
All: no neuron explanations checked against held-out firing.
All: no neuron-level simulation scores. The explain-and-predict scores are for experts only.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked r1–r3 to V2, but V2 concerns shares of neuron poles with one job. Expert-level scores are a different unit and a different metric (binary prediction accuracy, with no share of units counted as monosemantic), so I relinked them to none and dropped the V2 limits_scope label. The study does not cite either original source. Table 9's LDS values (0.687–0.708) are the only numeric score levels in the text and are a possible analogue for V7-type comparisons, but they are expert-level, so they appear under fits_no_version. The fine-tuning results were correctly left out.

versions.untested_parts: The Qwen3-32B audit, neuron poles, and the proportions with one job, two related jobs, or not-yet-understood jobs.

The study measures expert-level scores in MoE models, not shares of neuron poles. It does not test dense models, models up to trillions of parameters, or whether similar proportions hold across models.
InceptionV1 cat-and-car neurons, pose detection, and recursive generalization versus superposition.
Late-layer neurons in InceptionV1-sized vision models, the proposed architecture and regularization explanation, and the stated interpretability estimates.
Attribution graphs built from a large model's neurons and reconstruction error.
Whether neuron explanations based on activating examples fail to predict neuron firing.
The share of neurons receiving good automated activation-prediction scores.

rows.subject: Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507
rows.operation_detail: Varied the number of activated experts and measured layer-wise decoupling score (LDS), defined as the average expert monosemanticity score.

conditions.value: varied by changing k, the number of activated experts; exact values not stated

rows.measure: Layer-wise decoupling score (LDS), average EMS across experts in a layer
rows.value: Figure 3a; text reports that reducing sparsity consistently and substantially decreases LDS across all evaluated values of k.
rows.note: The textual description gives the direction of the trend, but numerical LDS values and exact k settings are not stated. The outcome varies with sparsity rather than establishing a stable cross-model share.
rows.check: Measures average expert-level explain-and-predict accuracy (LDS) as k varies in Qwen3-30B-A3B. This is not a share of neuron poles with one job, so it does not bear on V2. No numbers appear in the text, only Figure 3a. The 'dense LLMs have lower monosemanticity' remark is an extrapolation; no dense model was measured.

rows.subject: Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507

conditions.value: network depth; exact layer values not stated

rows.measure: Layer-wise decoupling score (LDS), average EMS across experts in a layer
rows.value: Figure 3b; text reports a rapid increase in early layers, a high middle-layer plateau, and a sharp decline near the output.
rows.note: The text says middle layers have the highest monosemanticity while input and output layers are nearly lowest; exact values are not stated.
rows.check: Expert-level LDS across depth in Qwen3-235B-A22B, read from Figure 3b only. This is an expert-level construct, not neuron-pole shares, so it does not link to V2.

rows.subject: Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507

rows.note: The authors describe coexistence of domain-specialized and shared experts; numeric score values are not stated in the text.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

relation.reason: The study applies its own explain-and-predict scoring (GPT-4o predicts activations) to MoE experts. It reports no neuron-level shares, so no version is tested.

tranche.reason: The study measures expert-level monosemanticity, which is a different construct from neuron poles. It uses those scores to choose experts for fine-tuning and tests no version. T6 is also defensible.

source_check.notes: Both rows come from figures only and measure experts, not neurons, so neither links to a version. Appendix A.10 compares expert and neuron explanations, but only qualitatively (Table 8), with no neuron-level scores. The claim that dense LLMs have lower monosemanticity is asserted from SAE literature and the k-to-N trend; dense models are not measured.
